paragraphs: Young Tamlane was the son of Earl Murray, and Burd Janet was the daughter of Dunbar, Earl of March. When they were young, they loved one another and promised to marry. But as their wedding drew near, Tamlane disappeared, and no one knew what had become of him.

Many, many days after he disappeared, Burd Janet was wandering in Carterhaugh Wood, although she had been warned not to go there. As she wandered, she picked flowers from the bushes. At last she came to a broom bush and began picking its flowers. She had taken no more than three little blossoms when young Tamlane suddenly appeared beside her.
“Where have you come from, Tamlane, Tamlane?” Burd Janet said. “And why have you been away so long?”
“I come from Elfland,” said young Tamlane. “The Queen of Elfland has made me her knight.”
“But how did you get there, Tamlane?” Burd Janet asked.

“I was hunting one day. As I rode anticlockwise around that hill, a deep drowsiness came over me. When I woke, there I was in Elfland. It is a beautiful, cheerful land, and I would gladly stay, except for you and one other thing. Every seven years, the Elves pay their tribute to the underworld. Although the Queen favours me, I fear I myself will be that tribute.”
“Oh, can’t you be saved? Tell me if there is anything I can do to save you, Tamlane.”

“There is only one way to save me. Tomorrow night is Halloween, when the fairy court will ride through England and Scotland. If you want to rescue me from Elfland, you must stand by Miles Cross between midnight and one in the morning. Take holy water in your hand and make a circle with it all around you.”
“But how will I know you, Tamlane,” Burd Janet asked, “among so many knights I have never seen before?”

“Let the first company of Elves pass. Show respect to the next company, but do nothing and say nothing. The third company is the chief court, and at its head rides the Queen of all Elfland. I shall ride beside her on a milk-white horse, with a star in my crown. They give me this honour because I am a baptised knight. Watch my hands, Janet. My right hand will be gloved, but my left will be bare. That is how you will know me.”
“But how do I save you, Tamlane?” Burd Janet asked.

“You must spring upon me suddenly, and I will fall to the ground. Then seize me quickly. Whatever happens to me, whatever shape I take—for they will use all their magic on me—hold tightly until they turn me into red-hot iron. Then throw me into this pool, and I will turn back into a man as naked as the day I was born. Throw your green cloak over me, and I shall be yours and belong to the world again.”
Burd Janet promised to do all this for Tamlane. The next night, at midnight, she took her place by Miles Cross and made a circle around herself with holy water.

Soon the Elfin court rode past. First a troop on black horses went over the mound, then another troop on brown horses. But in the third company, all riding milk-white horses, she saw the Queen of Elfland. Beside her rode a knight with a star in his crown, his right hand gloved and his left bare. Then she knew that this was her own Tamlane. Springing forward, she seized the milk-white horse’s bridle and pulled its rider down. As soon as he touched the ground, she let go of the bridle and caught him in her arms.
“He’s won, he’s won among us all!” shrieked the eerie company. They all gathered around her and tried their spells on young Tamlane.

First they made him like frozen ice in Janet’s arms, then changed him into a huge, roaring flame. Then the fire vanished, and an adder writhed through her arms, but still she held on. Next they turned him into a snake that reared up as though to bite her, yet she held on. Suddenly a dove struggled in her arms and almost flew away. They turned him into a swan, but it was all in vain. At last he became a red-hot sword. She threw it into a well of water, and he turned back into a man as naked as the day he was born. She quickly threw her green cloak over him, and young Tamlane belonged to Burd Janet for ever.
Then the Queen of Elfland sang as the court turned away and began to resume its procession:

“The woman who rescued young Tamlane
Has gained a splendid groom,
She’s taken my most handsome knight,
Left no one in his place.
“But had I known, Tamlane, Tamlane,
A lady would rescue you,
I’d have taken out your two grey eyes
And put in two of wood.
“Had I only known, Tamlane, Tamlane,
Before we left our home,
I’d have taken out your heart of flesh
And put in a heart of stone.
“If I had only known last night
What I know today,
I’d have paid the Devil seven times his due
Before you were won away.”
Then the Elfin court rode away, and Burd Janet and young Tamlane went home. They were married soon afterwards, once Tamlane had again been blessed with holy water and made Christian once more.
